section_summary: This section begins with extensive 1930–1931 correspondence about the destruction by fire of the Japan Advertiser, efforts to refinance and reorganize it, and official congratulations when publication resumed. Later papers concern threats against the newspaper during Japan’s 1932 war fever, State Department policy on supplying messages to foreign newspapers, and 1936 surveys of American news coverage in the Japanese press. The final documents report plans for a Japanese-controlled English-language newspaper in Tianjin and protest the Osaka Mainichi’s publication of ostensibly pro-Japanese remarks falsely attributed to former U.S. Military Attaché William Carey Crane.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 208 on the destruction of the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.about: Forbes reports the total destruction of the Japan Advertiser’s building and asks whether potential financial supporters can be approached.
subfiles.summary: The Japan Advertiser’s building and property had burned two days earlier and were a total loss. Forbes emphasizes the paper’s international usefulness and asks whether the Department can suggest a way to approach individuals or institutions, naming Lamont and Crane as already interested.

subfiles.title: Stimson message of sympathy to Fleisher
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Department of State
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo, for Benjamin W. Fleisher
subfiles.about: Stimson sends condolences and expresses hope that the Japan Advertiser will quickly resume publication.
subfiles.summary: Stimson regrets both Fleisher’s personal loss and the interruption of a newspaper important to Japanese-American understanding. He hopes the suspension will be brief and that Fleisher will soon continue publishing.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 211 seeking Egan’s encouragement
subfiles.about: Forbes asks Martin Egan to encourage Fleisher’s effort to restart the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports that insurance will cover debts to Lamont and other guarantors. Fleisher is willing to start again if adequate support can be found, and Forbes stresses the paper’s international importance.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Forbes’s telegram to Martin Egan
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Martin Egan, care of J. P. Morgan and Company
subfiles.about: Peck forwards a copy of Forbes’s telegram concerning the Japan Advertiser fire.
subfiles.summary: The letter encloses telegram No. 211 of November 7 from the American Ambassador in Tokyo. It identifies the subject as the destruction of the Japan Advertiser’s building and property.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Forbes’s cable to Egan
subfiles.about: Egan acknowledges receipt of Peck’s letter and Forbes’s cable.
subfiles.summary: Egan confirms receipt of the November 8 letter and the enclosed cable from Ambassador Cameron Forbes. He thanks Peck for transmitting them.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 220 to Arthur Woods
subfiles.about: Forbes endorses the Japan Advertiser’s management in anticipation of a possible request for assistance.
subfiles.summary: Forbes describes the newspaper’s destroyed plant and its recognized value in promoting international understanding. He assures Woods of his support for the management and notes that Ivy Lee has full information.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Forbes’s telegram to Arthur Woods
subfiles.about: The Department transmits a copy of Forbes’s November 17 telegram about the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: The OCR is largely illegible, but the page is a formal State Department transmittal associated with Forbes’s telegram to Arthur Woods. It concerns the paper’s destruction and possible financial support.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 223 urging use of insurance funds
subfiles.about: Forbes urges the guarantors to permit insurance proceeds to be used to reestablish the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: Forbes believes Fleisher must obtain a new plant and asks the Equitable guarantors to allow the insurance money to finance reconstruction. He says that increasing the guarantee by twenty-five percent would ensure the newspaper’s survival.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Telegram No. 223
subfiles.from: Willys R. Peck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.to: Martin Egan, care of J. P. Morgan and Company
subfiles.about: Peck forwards Forbes’s November 19 telegram about the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: The letter encloses a copy of telegram No. 223 from the American Ambassador in Tokyo. It again identifies the subject as the fire that destroyed the newspaper’s building and property.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Telegram No. 223
subfiles.about: Egan acknowledges receipt of Forbes’s November 19 cable.
subfiles.summary: Egan confirms receiving Peck’s November 20 letter and the enclosed cable from Ambassador Forbes. He thanks Peck for both.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on further Department action
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Hornbeck reviews Forbes’s messages and considers whether Castle or Stimson should personally contact the financiers.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck notes that Telegram No. 225 asks whether Castle has seen earlier messages to Woods and Egan and whether their principals favor renewing the loan. He believes the Department as an institution can do little beyond transmitting the telegrams, though Castle or the Secretary might telephone the interested parties.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 225 asking about the loan
subfiles.about: Forbes asks whether Woods’s and Egan’s principals favor renewing the Japan Advertiser loan.
subfiles.summary: Forbes refers Castle to his earlier telegrams sent for Woods and Egan. He requests information about their principals’ attitude toward continuing the loan.

subfiles.title: Castle’s reply on Egan and Woods
subfiles.about: Castle reports that Egan considers renewal impossible and that Woods has not yet been reached.
subfiles.summary: Egan says the bank cannot continue carrying a frozen loan and that Rockefeller’s absence in Europe complicates matters. Castle promises to see Woods the following week and reiterates the desire to help.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 230 protesting liquidation consequences
subfiles.about: Forbes argues that liquidation would unfairly harm Japanese creditors and permanently close the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports Egan’s cable announcing the New York backers’ refusal to extend the Equitable loan. He argues that access to the insurance money would let Fleisher rebuild and perhaps sell the paper, whereas immediate liquidation would pay American interests while sharply reducing payments to Japanese interests and dispersing the staff.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 229 to Martin Egan
subfiles.about: Forbes assures Egan that no one disputes the first mortgage’s priority and defends Fleisher’s standing.
subfiles.summary: Forbes says nothing in the recent cables questions full payment of the Equitable first mortgage. He expresses surprise at the financiers’ dissatisfaction, calls Fleisher and the newspaper first-rate, and reports Fleisher’s confidence that a rebuilt paper could be sold for about twice the insurance proceeds.

subfiles.title: Castle letter explaining the Department’s interest
subfiles.about: Castle relays Forbes’s arguments while disclaiming any Department role in the financial decision.
subfiles.summary: Castle summarizes Forbes’s view that rebuilding could preserve value, protect Japanese interests, and allow an eventual sale. He states that the Department cannot advise Egan on the finances but emphasizes the Japan Advertiser’s importance to American interests and good relations in Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 233 correcting creditor information
subfiles.about: Forbes corrects his description of which Japanese claims would suffer in liquidation.
subfiles.summary: Fleisher explains that Japanese second-mortgage holders are protected by insurance. The endangered claims are unsecured notes, current expenses, salaries, and discharge allowances.

subfiles.title: Egan’s confidential explanation of the loan decision
subfiles.about: Egan confidentially explains why Lamont and the other guarantors cannot further support Fleisher.
subfiles.summary: Egan says Lamont’s guarantee was an act of friendship after the 1923 disaster, not an investment in the enterprise. The seven-year-old bank loan remains unreduced, has overdue interest, and has been criticized by examiners; Egan also describes Fleisher’s management as extravagant and cites severe New York financial conditions.

subfiles.title: Castle’s confidential acknowledgment to Egan
subfiles.about: Castle acknowledges Egan’s confidential account of the Japan Advertiser’s finances.
subfiles.summary: Castle promises to keep Egan’s information entirely confidential. Although sorry that the newspaper’s prospects are so poor, he says he understands Egan’s position.

subfiles.title: Confidential file slip
subfiles.about: The slip records that the associated material was filed in the confidential file.
subfiles.summary: The page contains only a confidential-file notation and the decimal file number. It marks the disposition of the preceding correspondence.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 246 on Japanese financial cooperation
subfiles.about: Forbes reports that Finance Minister Inoue may mobilize Japanese support if American capital and a sound business plan are secured.
subfiles.summary: Inoue, Baron Dan, and others regard resumption of the Japan Advertiser as extremely important. Inoue supports creating a business advisory committee, and Forbes asks Geary, Place, and DeVault to serve with Fleisher’s cooperation.

subfiles.title: Castle forwards the advisory-committee proposal
subfiles.about: Castle sends Forbes’s advisory-committee proposal to Egan for consideration.
subfiles.summary: Castle wonders whether Fleisher’s willingness to accept an advisory committee might change the New York financing situation. He identifies Geary as General Electric’s capable Japan chief, describes DeVault as an excellent consul at Yokohama, and says he knows nothing about Place.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on the November 4 fire
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a report on the November 4 destruction of the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: The document points to a report dated December 2, 1930. Its stated subject is the fire that destroyed the newspaper on November 4.

subfiles.title: Report excerpt on the Japan Advertiser fire
subfiles.about: The excerpt describes the fire’s effect on the foreign community and estimates the loss.
subfiles.summary: The November 4 fire destroyed Japan’s only American-owned newspaper, on which much of the English-speaking foreign community depended for news and American opinion. Faulty electrical wiring was suspected, and the loss was estimated at ¥1,200,000, largely insured.

subfiles.title: Egan letter on discussions with Jerome Greene
subfiles.about: Egan promises to explore Japan Advertiser financing possibilities with Jerome Greene.
subfiles.summary: Egan acknowledges Castle’s December 12 letter and says Jerome Greene has told him about Castle’s message. Although uncertain that anything can be achieved, Egan and Greene intend to explore every possibility.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 264 proposing an approach to Crane and the President
subfiles.about: Forbes recommends directly asking Charles R. Crane for support and informing the President.
subfiles.summary: Forbes suggests telephoning Crane to ask how much financing he will personally take and how much he can place elsewhere. He also recommends bringing the dossier of communications to the President’s attention.

subfiles.title: Castle cable reporting Lamont’s conditional interest
subfiles.about: Castle reports that Lamont might reconsider if an excellent financial manager were appointed.
subfiles.summary: Lamont says that competent financial management would create a new situation deserving sympathetic consideration. Castle has also written directly to Crane and contacted other people in New York.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 263 presenting the reorganization plan
subfiles.about: Forbes reports the advisory committee’s financial assessment and its proposal for a new American company.
subfiles.summary: The committee values assets at ¥507,800 against ¥505,000 in secured and unsecured debts and believes insurance and other assets can pay all creditors. It forecasts minimum annual earnings of ¥50,000 and proposes a new American company capitalized at $150,000 through preference shares. Forbes recommends common shares for Fleisher’s goodwill and continued editorial role, while noting that some financing might be raised in Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 7 accepting financial supervision
subfiles.about: Forbes reports that Fleisher accepts outside financial supervision and could resume quickly if supported.
subfiles.summary: Fleisher agrees to whatever supervisory conditions Lamont and the other financiers require. If adequate backing is assured, he can restart the newspaper within two weeks.

subfiles.title: Wasserman letter enclosing his financing proposal
subfiles.about: Wasserman forwards his letter to Egan and says Rockefeller’s continued credit could complete the financing.
subfiles.summary: Wasserman encloses a copy of his January 16 proposal to Martin Egan. He believes that securing Rockefeller’s $50,000 credit would resolve the remaining difficulty.

subfiles.title: Wasserman’s detailed recapitalization proposal
subfiles.about: Wasserman proposes a debt-free new company with secured financing, family capital, and independent business management.
subfiles.summary: The plan calls for $100,000 in serial mortgage lien notes and $75,000 in preferred stock, with Fleisher’s family pledging the preferred capital. Fleisher would receive 45 percent of the common stock and retain editorial control, while Merritt Hulburd or another manager would control finances and might eventually obtain a controlling interest. Wasserman argues that this structure would preserve Fleisher’s Japanese relationships while correcting the old company’s weak financial management.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 12 requesting news of the project
subfiles.about: Forbes asks for an update because delay is undermining the Japan Advertiser project.
subfiles.summary: Forbes says time is running heavily against the proposed revival. He reports that Inouye has strongly endorsed the newspaper’s necessity to Ramsey, representing Harris, Forbes, then affiliated with Chase Bank.

subfiles.title: Castle night letter to Martin Egan
subfiles.about: Castle summarizes the available family capital, management safeguards, and Forbes’s latest appeal.
subfiles.summary: Castle reports that Wasserman has raised $75,000 from Fleisher’s family, secured a prospective independent manager, and arranged for Tokyo committee supervision. He says that continuing $50,000 of the old loan would permit immediate resumption and repeats Inouye’s endorsement to Ramsey.

subfiles.title: Wasserman’s update after the Rockefeller refusal
subfiles.about: Wasserman reports Rockefeller’s refusal but remains hopeful that Lamont, Crane, and Japanese investors can finance the paper.
subfiles.summary: After discussing the matter with John D. Rockefeller III, Wasserman accepts that Rockefeller’s objections are reasonable. He awaits Lamont’s decision through Egan, expects Crane to cooperate, believes the family can raise $75,000 and Japan another $50,000, and plans to see Richard Waldo.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 15 offering a Tokyo finance committee
subfiles.about: Forbes offers to organize a strong local committee and assist in finding a business manager.
subfiles.summary: Forbes says a strong finance committee can be secured in Japan and can also serve as directors if desired. The group could help select a business manager and strengthen the financing effort.

subfiles.title: Illegible Far Eastern Affairs memorandum
subfiles.about: The largely illegible memorandum appears in the file immediately after Forbes’s January 30 financing telegram.
subfiles.summary: Only the Department and division headings are clearly readable. The remaining handwritten or degraded text cannot be reliably reconstructed from the OCR.

subfiles.title: Telegram conveying Stimson’s greeting for resumed publication
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Department of State
subfiles.to: American Embassy, Tokyo, for Benjamin W. Fleisher
subfiles.about: Stimson welcomes the Japan Advertiser’s reappearance and congratulates Fleisher.
subfiles.summary: The message calls the newspaper an institution in Far Eastern news gathering, interpretation, and dissemination. Stimson and other Department officers interested in the Far East congratulate Fleisher on his courage and enterprise.

subfiles.title: Draft congratulatory telegram to Fleisher
subfiles.about: The draft formulates an official welcome for the revived newspaper.
subfiles.summary: It describes the Japan Advertiser as an institution in Far Eastern journalism and welcomes its reappearance. The draft congratulates Fleisher on his renewed courage and enterprise.

subfiles.title: Secretary’s request for a draft greeting
subfiles.about: Hornbeck is asked to have his division prepare a personal greeting for the Secretary.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary wants a personal line of greeting drafted that afternoon. The request initiates preparation of the message for the revived Japan Advertiser.

subfiles.title: Reminder concerning Wile’s request
subfiles.about: The note reminds the Secretary to act on Fred Wile’s request before departing.
subfiles.summary: A copy of the Secretary’s earlier message to Fleisher is attached for reference. Wile needs the new statement in Tokyo by March 26.

subfiles.title: Assistant Secretary’s note on Wile’s request
subfiles.about: The note reports Wile and Fleisher’s desire for a statement marking the Japan Advertiser’s resumption.
subfiles.summary: Wile seeks a statement for the resumed publication and says Fleisher is particularly anxious to receive it. Wile has offered to receive a collect cable.

subfiles.title: Wile’s letter to Henry L. Stimson
subfiles.about: Wile asks Stimson for a personal greeting for the Japan Advertiser’s March 26 relaunch.
subfiles.summary: Wile reports that Fleisher will resume publication after the November fire, the paper’s second destruction following the 1923 earthquake. He requests a few words for the first post-disaster issue.

subfiles.title: Wile’s letter to William R. Castle Jr.
subfiles.about: Wile asks Castle for a greeting to the revived Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: The letter repeats that Fleisher is restarting publication on March 26 after the November fire. Wile emphasizes Fleisher’s second recovery from disaster and requests a short message for the new issue.

subfiles.title: Wile’s letter to Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Wile asks Hornbeck for a greeting for the newspaper’s first issue after the fire.
subfiles.summary: Wile describes Fleisher’s effort as heroic and recalls that the paper had also been destroyed in the 1923 earthquake. He requests a short personal greeting that can be cabled to Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Revised draft greeting to Fleisher
subfiles.about: The revised draft welcomes the Japan Advertiser’s return and congratulates Fleisher.
subfiles.summary: The language closely follows the final Stimson message, calling the paper an institution in Far Eastern journalism. It offers congratulations on Fleisher’s courage and enterprise.

subfiles.title: Reply to Wile enclosing the sent telegram
subfiles.about: The Department informs Wile that a message has been sent through the American Ambassador in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges Wile’s three March 19 requests to Stimson, Castle, and Hornbeck. It encloses a copy of the telegram prepared for publication in the Japan Advertiser’s March 26 issue.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to confidential despatch on hostility toward the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.about: The sheet points to Forbes’s confidential report on violent anti-Advertiser feeling in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch is dated March 9, 1932. Its stated subject is violent feeling in Japan against the Japan Advertiser.

subfiles.title: Fragment of confidential despatch on threats against the Japan Advertiser
subfiles.about: The fragment reports political rumors, police warnings, and threats of mob violence against Fleisher and the Japan Advertiser.
subfiles.summary: Amid rumors about Baron Shidehara’s health, police warned Fleisher that patriotic extremists might attack the newspaper after it printed photographs from China. Shiratori denounced the United States, while Forbes advised Fleisher to approach Yoshizawa and asked McIlroy to explain to the Army the damage an attack would do Japan. Police protection was sought for the Fleisher homes, though Fleisher later said he did not expect personal danger.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to despatch on moderating Japanese newspapers
subfiles.about: The sheet references a despatch reporting a more reasonable attitude by several Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.summary: The referenced publications are the Jiji Shimpo, Hochi Shimbun, and Japan Times and Mail. The despatch says they had become more moderate toward American policy in the Far East.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on a proposed presidential message to Fleisher
subfiles.about: Beck reports the President’s instruction that the Secretary decide whether a presidential message should be sent.
subfiles.summary: Rudolph Forster says Wile requested a message from the President and that the White House sought instructions by wireless. The President replied that the Secretary of State should decide and, if favorable, arrange an appropriate message.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum opposing an additional presidential message
subfiles.about: Hornbeck advises that Stimson’s message is sufficient and that the President need not send another.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck reasons that the President referred the matter to the Secretary without expressly asking for a message in his own name. He argues that presidential messages to private publications should be reserved for clearly exceptional cases to avoid favoritism or an obligation to honor all similar requests.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on foreign-publication message policy
subfiles.from: Stanley K. Hornbeck, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Hornbeck endorses established precedents against supplying messages to individual foreign publications.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says similar requests arise repeatedly in Far Eastern Affairs and presumably in other regional divisions. He supports the positions taken in Frank B. Kellogg’s 1925 letter to Wile and a 1928 instruction to Neville.

subfiles.title: Iwamoto request for a New Year’s message
subfiles.about: Iwamoto requests a 500-word statement on American-Japanese relations for the Hochi Shimbun’s New Year issue.
subfiles.summary: Writing as the American representative of Shimbun Rengosha, Iwamoto transmits the request of its member newspaper. He asks for an early reply and hopes to receive the article by November 28.

subfiles.title: Phillips declines the Hochi Shimbun invitation
subfiles.from: William Phillips, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Phillips declines to provide a message because of Department policy toward individual foreign publications.
subfiles.summary: Phillips acknowledges the opportunity to discuss relations between the United States and Japan and says he would otherwise be pleased to accept. He explains that the practice of withholding messages or articles from individual foreign newspapers or agencies requires him to decline.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Nagoya news survey
subfiles.about: The sheet references a consular report surveying news coverage in Nagoya.
subfiles.summary: The referenced report is dated August 17, 1936. Its stated subject is a survey of American news carried in the Nagoya press.

subfiles.title: Survey of American news in the Nagoya press
subfiles.from: Charles H. Stephan, American Vice Consul, Nagoya
subfiles.about: Stephan reports on the quantity and character of American news distributed to Nagoya newspapers.
subfiles.summary: The local Domei branch and Shin Aichi could not quantify five years of coverage but agreed that both the number and space of American items had increased. They estimated that American material formed half of all foreign news and that more than sixty percent of it concerned commerce and trade. The report also explains Domei’s formation from Nippon Dempo Tsushinsha and Rengo Tsushinsha and identifies its American wire-service sources.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Tokyo press survey
subfiles.about: The sheet references Despatch No. 2023 on American news in the Japanese press.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch is dated September 3, 1936. Its subject is a survey of American news items appearing in the local press.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2023 surveying American news in Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch analyzes the volume, sources, recent decline, and subject matter of American news in Japanese newspapers.
subfiles.summary: The survey estimates that foreign news occupies only a small portion of Japanese newspaper space and that American items form a still smaller share, with Domei serving as the principal distributor. American coverage had declined slightly since 1931 because bilateral tensions had eased, European developments under Hitler and Mussolini had become more dramatic, and the merger creating Domei reduced competitive wire coverage. Japanese readers remained interested chiefly in American markets, business, policies directly affecting Japan, natural disasters, crime, and selected sports or celebrity news, while showing little interest in routine American politics.

subfiles.title: Department copy of report on a Japanese-controlled newspaper in Tianjin
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul, Dalian
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grummon reports plans to establish a Japanese-controlled English-language newspaper in Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: The proposed paper would support Japanese aspirations in North China and would reportedly resemble the officially favored Manchuria Daily News. Its editorship had allegedly been offered to O’Neil Tane, a Canadian assistant editor at that newspaper.

subfiles.title: Duplicate consular copy on the Tianjin newspaper project
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul, Dalian
subfiles.to: Erle R. Dickover, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: This duplicate copy reports the planned Japanese-sponsored English newspaper in Tianjin.
subfiles.summary: Grummon repeats that Japanese interests expect to create an English paper in Tianjin modeled on the Manchuria Daily News. O’Neil Tane is identified as the prospective editor, and copies are designated for diplomatic posts in China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1 protesting remarks attributed to Crane
subfiles.about: Grew reports his protest over the Osaka Mainichi’s publication of supposedly unneutral remarks attributed to William Carey Crane.
subfiles.summary: The Osaka Mainichi issued a pamphlet, “Common Sense and the China Emergency,” quoting the former military attaché in terms that appeared pro-Japanese and unneutral. Grew showed the Foreign Minister Crane’s prior request that the comments not be published and called the publication unethical and grossly unjust. The minister promised appropriate action.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on Despatch No. 2724
subfiles.about: The memorandum notes that Grew’s telegram had already covered the Crane controversy and that the despatch merely supplies details and documents.
subfiles.summary: The office considers the matter of the falsely attributed unneutral remarks adequately reported by telegram. Despatch No. 2724 amplifies the record and documents Grew’s expression of extreme annoyance to the Japanese Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2724 on remarks falsely attributed to Lieutenant-Colonel Crane
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The opening of the despatch documents how the Osaka Mainichi published pro-Japanese statements that Crane denied making.
subfiles.summary: After the Japan Advertiser announced the forthcoming Osaka Mainichi pamphlet, Crane wrote its editor on November 22, 1937, denying that he had discussed restoration of order in North China and asking that the supposed comments be withheld. Major Saito of the Japanese War Office promised to seek suppression, but the pamphlet nevertheless appeared and attributed praise of Japanese rule and restored order to Crane. The despatch continues beyond page 80.
